principle: Declarations sharing a namespace are grouped under a `namespace` command, and a name is written without a namespace prefix that an enclosing `namespace` or `open` already supplies.
A computable definition or `Decidable` instance is implemented by an efficient algorithm, not by a direct transcription of its specification (the quantifier structure of the proposition).
A lemma whose left-hand side applies a definition to a canonical argument and whose right-hand side is simpler is tagged `@[simp]`.
The general core of a specific result is extracted as its own declaration about the underlying general construction, and the specific result is derived from it.
A goal that a standard finishing tactic (`simp`, `rfl`, `trivial`, `omega`, `positivity`, `grind`, `grw`, ...) closes is closed by that tactic, not by a hand-written term or rewrite chain.
A new declaration reuses the `variable`s already declared in the file rather than introducing duplicates of them.

A hypothesis, conclusion or expression that matches a library-named predicate or function is written with that name, not as its unfolded definition, a lambda, the negation of its complement, or an ad hoc encoding.
A new definition or instance comes with the lemmas that characterise its value, so that it is never unfolded by hand at use sites.
A structure instance is written with `where` syntax rather than the anonymous constructor, `{ ... }` notation, or a tactic-mode `constructor`.
A hypothesis that the definition or proof does not need is dropped, or weakened to what it does need, so that the result holds in the greater generality.
A result or construction that existing library lemmas or API yield directly (a composition of library equivalences) is derived from them, not reproved or rebuilt from first principles.
A `namespace`, `section`, `end` or `variable` command is separated from the declarations and commands around it by a blank line.
An auxiliary `have` or `let` whose proof is a short term is inlined at its use sites rather than named.

A `simp` call that is terminal, or whose output feeds only a flexible finishing tactic, is not squeezed to `simp only`; the explicit lemma list is reserved for calls whose exact output a later step depends on.
An object of a structure that extends another is constructed directly with all its fields, not by first defining the parent structure as a separate declaration.
A `simp` call does not list lemmas that are already in the default simp set.
Syntax that elaboration supplies on its own, such as an explicit coercion, a type ascription or redundant parentheses, is omitted.
Consecutive tactic calls or `calc` steps that a single call can perform are merged into that one call.
A lemma's name is built from the names of every declaration in its statement, spelled as those declarations spell them, not from informal synonyms, re-tokenisations or omissions.
A typeclass hypothesis is left anonymous and retrieved with `‹_›` or by inference rather than bound to a name.
A construction that can conflict with a non-definitionally-equal instance on the same type is a `def`, not an `instance`.

A recurring collection of lemmas passed to `simp` together is registered as a named simp set (simp attribute) and called by that name, rather than listed lemma by lemma or with `attribute [local simp]` in each file.
A categorical or order-theoretic lemma is accompanied by its dual statement.

An automation call such as `grind`, or a flexible `simp` in place of a squeezed `simp only`, replaces an explicit proof only when the explicit proof is not short and readable and the automation is not markedly slower.
A module docstring's title states precisely what the file proves, not a generic heading that suggests a different or broader result.
A definition is `abbrev` only when downstream elaboration or instance search needs it to unfold; otherwise it is a `def`.
A special case of a general lemma that is the common use, with the hypothesis that simplifies the statement, is stated as its own lemma.

A characterisation lemma is also stated in the variant form (indexing set, coercion, side-condition shape, direction of rewriting, or pointwise application of a bundled map) in which users will apply it.
A docstring explains the declaration on its own terms rather than by contrast with another declaration.
A file does not import a module it does not need or that another of its imports already provides.
A structure's fields and projections are named after the library's established names for the same role in analogous structures.
When a declaration's signature spans lines, the break comes after the colon so that the conclusion starts on its own line, not in the middle of the conclusion.

A result that follows from a stronger structural statement (an equivalence, isomorphism, adjunction or one-sided inverse) is derived from that statement, which is stated and proved as its own declaration.
A function whose namespace is determined by the expected type is written with leading-dot notation (`.congr`) rather than its full name.
Two lemmas that are both immediate projections of one stronger statement are replaced by that stronger statement.
An argument's binder kind follows inferability: one that the other explicit arguments or later hypotheses determine is implicit, and one that cannot be inferred from them is explicit.
A declaration whose short name would clash with a root-namespace name when its namespace is opened is `protected`.
A PR written with AI assistance follows the AI contribution guidelines: it discloses that, and how, in its description.
A change to the observable output of meta-code (message severity, format) is checked against the tools that consume it.
A short tactic block that a single term proves is written as that term.
A new concept, a new lemma whose use is not evident, or a design change comes with motivation, in the module docstring or PR description, saying why it is useful and how it will be used.
A tactic reuses the existing binder and argument syntax and parsers rather than introducing its own variant.

A PR is cut at its natural seams: separable parts, whether a core and its extensions or a part needing more design work, are split so each is reviewed on its own, and parts that only make sense together are not split arbitrarily.
A docstring's closing `-/` follows the last line of text directly, on that line, with no blank line before it and not on a line of its own.
The module docstring is kept in step with the code: it covers every main result the file contains, as currently stated.
A `match` over a closed inductive type lists every constructor explicitly rather than ending with a catch-all case.
Lambda abstractions are written with `fun` and `↦`, not `λ` or `=>`.
Arguments shared by consecutive declarations are declared once with `variable`, not repeated in each signature.
A result whose converse also holds is stated as an iff.
An `open` that repeats a namespace already open in scope, or that nothing in its scope uses, is removed.
A new file is imported in `Mathlib.lean`.
A new file is a `module` with its content in an `@[expose] public section` unless a smaller public API is deliberately curated.
A cleanup PR leaves out a hunk whose change costs more readability than the cleanup gains.
A term whose type already matches the goal is used as is, not wrapped in a normalising tactic (`by simpa using`, `by exact`).
An instance that typeclass inference already finds is not declared; at most it is kept as an `example`.
A file-level directive such as `set_option linter.style.longFile` is placed where the library's other files place it.
A namespaced function or lemma applied to a term of that namespace's type is written with dot notation (`x.f`), not the fully qualified name.

A structure transferred along an injective map or a faithful functor is obtained from the library's general transfer construction (`Function.Injective.*`, `Monoidal.induced`), added if missing, not proved by hand.

Punctuation, operators and application inside terms, and text in docstrings, carry the standard spacing: a space after commas in tuples and lists, around infix operators (`/`, `^`), around `:=` in named arguments and inside structure-instance braces, inside set-builder braces (`{ x | p x }`), around `|` in alternative patterns, and after `←` in a rewrite list, none after an opening bracket or a prefix `-`, one after a markdown heading marker, and never a doubled space or a trailing space at the end of a line or string.
The direct lemma for a goal is used rather than one obtained by converting another (`le_rfl`, not `rfl.le`).
A class or structure whose axioms follow from a smaller set of conditions under extra structure gets a constructor taking only those conditions.
A `refine` or `apply` that leaves no goals is written as `exact`.

A result stated for a concrete type, object or value (a specific filter, a default element) but using only an abstract property of it, or none, is stated for every type, object or value with that property.
A lambda applied to an argument is written beta-reduced.
A goal is brought to the required form, or closed, by rewriting with the relevant lemmas rather than by `change`, `show`, `reduce` or `rfl` across a definitional equality.
Intermediate states or types recorded as comments in a term are expressed in the code itself, with `calc`, `trans` or type ascriptions.
A tool that proposes replacement syntax presents it in the standard `Try this:` form.
A recurring conjunction of hypotheses on an object is bundled as a Prop-valued class so that results take it as an instance argument.
Continuation lines of a declaration's statement are indented four spaces.
A lemma's name spells the terms of its statement in head-first reading order: function before argument, left-hand side before relation before right-hand side, hypotheses in the order they appear.
A lemma connecting two topics is placed in the file of the topic that already carries the heavier imports, so the more basic file does not acquire them.
A declaration removed or moved in a refactor is deprecated with its replacement rather than deleted outright.
A deprecation, or a documentation note that a declaration is obsolete, names the replacement and, when it is not a drop-in substitute, says how to use it.
Material that is off a file's topic, or that would add heavy imports to it, goes in the file, and directory, where it belongs or a new one.
A workaround (`set_option ... in`, `erw`) is scoped to the declaration or rewrite step that needs it, not set for the whole file or applied to a whole rewrite chain.
A workaround (`set_option`, `erw`, `backward.*` options) is re-checked against current master and removed if no longer needed.
A goal is not closed by a chain of alternating flexible normalisation tactics (`simp`, `norm_num`, `ring_nf`); it is rewritten with the relevant lemmas and closed by a single normaliser.

A hypothesis, a non-obvious construct such as a private import or a workaround, or a non-obvious mathematical claim in documentation, whose necessity or truth is not evident, is justified by a reference or a comment.
A data-valued goal in an impossible case is produced by an explicit `absurd` or `False.elim` from the contradiction, not by a tactic closing the goal directly.
Tests for an additive or dual version of a tactic mirror every test of the original that has an analogue.

When an attribute, modifier (`protected`) or elaborator (`fast_instance%`) is applied to some of a family of sibling declarations but not others, either it is applied to all or a comment records why the others are excluded.
A deprecated declaration is kept only as a one-line derivation from its replacement; its old proof is deleted.
The equations of a family of lemmas about one map, and of the analogous lemmas across sibling structures, point in one consistent direction, which is the `simp` normal form.
A line is broken when, and only when, it exceeds the 100-character limit; a call, short proof, one-line declaration with its attribute, or docstring that fits on one line stays on one line.
A refactor of meta-code preserves its exact behaviour, including corner cases, unless the change is intended and stated.
A new predicate, definition or lemma is not introduced when an existing library declaration already expresses or states it.
A lemma whose hypotheses vary two things at once is split into the one-sided lemmas, from which the combined version follows.
A tactic block after `=>` is written without enclosing braces.
Arguments that elaboration can infer from the expected type or from the other arguments are not passed explicitly (`_`, `..`, or a redundant named argument).
A definition producing data is written as a term, by pattern matching where needed, not as a tactic block.
The Mathlib repository is not used to test automated scripts or tools; a PR is a contribution intended to be merged.
In do-notation, a monadic result consumed by a single `match` is matched on directly (`match ← e with`) rather than first bound to an intermediate variable.
Meta-code that matches on the shape of an expression uses `match_expr`, not raw constructor patterns (`mkApp`, `.const`).
A monotonicity or congruence step in an inequality is discharged by `gcongr`, not by applying the specific named monotonicity lemma.

A congruence lemma for a predicate under eventual equality is stated as an implication taking the predicate as its first hypothesis, named `congr_of_eventuallyEq`, following the library's pattern, not as an iff.
The body of a `match`, `cases` or `induction` alternative is indented two spaces past its `|`, not further.
Tactics, and the alternatives of a `cases`/`induction`/`match`, are written one per line; `;` is not used to put several tactics on one line.
A declaration that is moved, generalised or deduplicated keeps exactly the attributes of the original, transferred to its replacement; attributes are not added or dropped in the process.
An attribute goes on its own line above a declaration whose header spans several lines, not inline before the keyword.

A variant or improvement introduced for one member of a family of siblings (left/right or primed lemma variants, analogous tactics or attributes, parallel code paths in meta-code) is also provided for the other members.
Commented-out code, scaffolding notes and working comments to oneself are removed before merging.
An instance that inference finds only after unfolding the type is given as `inferInstanceAs <unfolded type>`, not by a tactic block (`dsimp`/`change` then `infer_instance`).
A new predicate or definition ships in the same PR with the basic API that motivated it (closure under unions, interaction lemmas), not the definition alone.
A relation between two bundled maps is stated as an equality of the maps themselves (through the appropriate projection), from which the pointwise version follows, rather than only pointwise.

A variable is named with the letter the file's area uses for its kind (`X`, `Y` for measurable spaces), not with a letter that has an established different meaning there (`ε` for a small real in analysis), or that is easily confused with another symbol (`O` with `0`).
An equation is stated in one direction only; the symmetric form is obtained with `.symm`, not stated as its own lemma.
A definition or proof taken from, or whose conventions follow, a published source cites that source in its docstring.

A declaration whose main argument is a term of type `T` or a hypothesis `P x`, or whose conclusion is `P x` when no argument is, is placed in `T`'s or `P`'s namespace so that it is applied with dot notation (`h.f` or `.of_h`).

Side goals that a short tactic closes are discharged inline in a `refine` or `apply` (`(by fun_prop)`), leaving `?_` for the real goal, rather than handled afterwards as separate bullets or with `any_goals`/`try` combinators.
A new declaration that formalises a notion the library already names is given that established name, so that the two are seen as one.
The docstring of a definition describes the value defined, as a noun phrase, not the act of computing it.
Nested lambdas `fun a ↦ fun b ↦ e` are written with a single binder list `fun a b ↦ e`.
A lemma variant is distinguished from its siblings by naming the term of its statement that differs, not by appending primes.
A lemma or auxiliary definition that exposes the implementation of an instance or definition, which users are not meant to rely on, is `private`.
A notation or instance is not introduced when a `@[simp]` lemma immediately rewrites it away; either the notation is the simp normal form or it is not defined.
A structure is built directly from the data at hand, not by first building an equivalent object and converting; the intermediate object is dropped.
A lemma whose formal statement does not read as its mathematical meaning (filters, encodings) carries a docstring stating that meaning in words.
When a statement is broken at a binary operator or arrow, the operator ends the line rather than starting the next.

A step, hypothesis or argument that the proof or program does not need (a rewrite after the goal already closes, an unused `have`, a lemma the tactic does not use, a check another step already performs) is removed.
A result about a binary operation (union, sup, product) that holds for the indexed version is stated for the indexed version, from which the binary one follows.
A lemma superseded by a general API is deprecated to its general counterpart, not redirected to another local lemma that is itself redundant.
A structure's underlying function or set is accessed through its registered coercion, not through the raw projection (`.1`, `.val`, `.toFun`).
A lemma that trades one notion for another with neither side simpler is not tagged `@[simp]`; the simp normal form of a notion is chosen deliberately, not lemma by lemma.
A structure whose equality is determined by its fields is tagged `@[ext]` at its declaration, not given a `local ext` attribute where needed.
A docstring is written in full sentences ending in a period.
The same construct or notation is spelled the same way throughout a file, in code and in docstrings (`have` vs `haveI`, one lambda arrow, one attribute placement, one notation for an interval).
A definition, or a `have` inside a proof whose statement is not evident from its term, states its type explicitly rather than leaving it to be inferred from the body.

A structure instance or long term that does not fit after `:=` starts on the next line indented two spaces, with its fields one per line and aligned under each other; fields are not packed several to a line unless the whole instance fits on one.
When a `simps`-generated lemma's right-hand side is a `match`, it is replaced by one hand-stated `@[simp]` lemma per case.
A lemma's name states its conclusion; a hypothesis or an argument's type appears in it (`_of_h`, `set_`) only when needed to distinguish it from a sibling.
A long proof embedded in a definition or instance field is extracted into a (possibly `private`) auxiliary lemma, even if used only once.
A bibliographic reference in a docstring points to the precise location (chapter, section, theorem number) in the source.

A `simp` or `norm_num` whose result is consumed by another tactic, including one hidden in `simpa using by tac`, is squeezed to `simp only [...]` or its lemmas are passed to the finishing tactic directly.
A `conv` target is selected by pattern (`conv in pat =>`) rather than by positional navigation (`lhs`, `rhs`, `enter`).
A module docstring uses only the standard section headings (Main definitions, Main results, Implementation notes, References, Tags); ad hoc headers are not added.
The file header's copyright year and Authors line, and the PR's co-author credits, record who actually wrote the material and when, listing everyone who contributed substantially.
When an expression is broken across lines, each continuation line is indented two spaces further than the line it continues, so indentation follows nesting depth.
A change of marginal benefit (cosmetic spacing, docstring polish) is not made, or not merged, when its review cost exceeds the gain.

A comment or docstring is kept in step with the code: one whose content does not hold for the code as it stands (a TODO already done, an explanation that no longer applies, a use not yet made) is updated or removed, and a TODO that still applies is not removed.
New or changed meta-code (a tactic, attribute, command or syntax) comes with tests exercising the new behaviour.
A declaration's name follows the case convention of its kind: `UpperCamelCase` for types, structures and classes, `lowerCamelCase` for definitions, `snake_case` for theorems.
A definition's docstring explains each component of its result and each non-obvious parameter, not only the main one.
A lemma stating that an operation is monotone in an argument is tagged `@[gcongr]` so that `gcongr` can use it.
A term applied with `?_` holes is applied with `refine`, not `apply`; `apply` is used only when the remaining arguments are left to unification.
A hypothesis that a tactic picks up from the local context on its own (`simpa` closing by assumption) is not passed to it explicitly.
A change that replaces one proof method by another across many proofs (automation by explicit lemmas, or `simp` by `grind`) is accompanied by a benchmark the PR reports.
A file that is removed, or all of whose declarations are deprecated, is kept as a deprecated module (`deprecated_module`) pointing to its replacement, not deleted or left unmarked.
A definition whose intended API differs from its raw unfolding says so in its docstring, pointing to the lemma to use instead.
Hypotheses introduced by `induction` or `cases` are named in the `with` clause of the structured form, not recovered afterwards with `rename_i`.
A case split on a proposition that the hypotheses already decide is replaced by a `have` proving the actual case; the impossible branch is not written out.
A hypothesis whose components are always used separately is destructured when introduced (`obtain ⟨a, b⟩`), not projected with `.1` and `.2` afterwards.
A new notion or file is not given a name that has a different established meaning or is ambiguous with another; the full standard name is used.
An iff lemma whose directions are used separately comes with `alias ⟨_, _⟩` names for each direction, so both are usable with dot notation.
A lemma that merely instantiates, reshapes or combines existing lemmas, with no real simplification of the statement, is not added; the existing lemmas are used directly.
A bound, estimate or conclusion is stated in the sharpest form the proof gives, not weakened to a cruder one.
The PR title and description say precisely what the change is (what moves where, what is renamed to what), kept accurate as the PR evolves.
An iff lemma or an equation puts the compound or less basic side on the left and the simpler side on the right, the direction in which it rewrites.
A construct with established notation (`[[a, b]]` for `uIcc`, `‖x‖`, `∑`) is written with the notation, not the underlying function name.

A field, definition, `have` or lemma whose value is a function, or whose conclusion is a `∀` or an implication, is written with its binders or match alternatives directly after the name, not as `:= fun x ↦ ...`, `:= fun | ...`, or a `∀` or `→` statement followed by `intro`.
A statement is not written with `@` and `_` placeholders; the term is spelled so that elaboration fills the implicit arguments, adding a helper or notation if needed.
The tactic block of a proof is indented two spaces under its declaration, never flush left.
A type synonym introduced to carry different instances is a one-field structure, with constructor and projection as the conversions, not a `def` alias with equivs.
A declaration's body contains no blank lines; stages of a long proof are separated by comments, not empty lines.
An instance is given an explicit name only when its generated lemmas or later references need a readable name (one tagged `@[simps]`); otherwise it is left anonymous with the auto-generated name.
A fact established, or an object constructed, inside a proof that is of independent use, or not about the proof's specific objects, is extracted as its own (possibly `private`) lemma or definition.
A filter hypothesis or goal (`∀ᶠ`) is handled through the filter API (`.self_of_nhds`, `.mono`, `filter_upwards`) rather than unpacked by hand into an explicit set, ε or membership proof.
A structure instance that reuses the fields of an existing bundled object inherits them with `__ := obj`, not by restating each field.
A proof is not compressed into dense one-liners; an intricate argument is split into intermediate steps that read on their own.
An `omit` command is scoped with `in` to the declaration that needs it, never issued bare for the rest of a section.

A new definition that parallels an existing library notion is phrased in the same form as that notion (a filter characterisation where `IsCompact` uses one) and takes its arguments in the same shape and order (a `Finset` argument where `Finset.sum` takes one).
A bound variable that the body does not use is written `_` (or cleared with `-` in `rintro`), not given a name.
When two library lemmas state the same result, or one is a more useful reformulation of the other, the other is deprecated in favour of it rather than both being kept.
A lemma that moves a cast through an operation or identifies a cast of a constant is tagged `@[norm_cast]`.

A `simps` attribute names the projection to generate (`apply`), and the definition spells `toFun` explicitly, when the generated lemma would otherwise be over-applied or state a definitionally-abused type.
A variable conventionally denoted by a Greek letter is named with that letter (`μ`, `φ`), not its Latin transliteration (`mu`, `phi`).
A tactic test asserts the state it is meant to produce (`guard_target`, `guard_hyp`), not merely that the example closes.
A type synonym that exists to carry different instances stays opaque to typeclass search; it is not made reducible for instances.
Inside a tactic proof an instance is introduced with `have`; `haveI` and `letI` are reserved for term-mode positions where inlining is needed.
The principal data argument of a definition is explicit even when a later hypothesis argument determines it.
A docstring introduces every symbol it uses (`V_ o` for an ordinal `o`) rather than leaving a variable's kind to be guessed.
A long proof, or a non-obvious construction or step inside a proof or program, carries short comments saying what the strategy is or what the step is for.
A universally quantified statement whose bound variable a following hypothesis determines binds it strict-implicitly (`∀ ⦃x⦄, x ∈ s → ...`), not explicitly.
A linter exemption (a `noshake.json` entry, `nolint`, a `linter` option) is not added to silence a warning that can be fixed at its source.
Sibling goals closed by the same tactic script are dispatched together (`<;>`, `all_goals`, `exacts`), not by writing the script out once per goal.
A purely stylistic change to existing code or prose that the style guide does not mandate is left to the original author's taste, not made by a third party.
An attribute for a `@[to_additive]` declaration is passed as `to_additive (attr := ...)` so that the additive version receives it too.
The module docstring of a file introducing a notion states in words what the notion means before listing the results.
Every `section` or `namespace` is closed with a matching `end`, not left open to the end of the file.
A definition takes its morphism argument as a concrete bundled type (`RingEquiv`), not through a `FunLike`/`FooClass` typeclass; the class-generic form is reserved for lemmas.
A proof uses no heavier machinery than its statement needs, so the lemma can sit in the earliest file where its statement makes sense.

A lemma's statement, especially a `@[simp]` right-hand side, and a simproc's output are in simp-normal form: they contain no subterm that `simp` would rewrite (`1`, not `exp 0`; a literal, not `n % 4`).
A docstring that names a theorem (`The Rees theorem`) also states what the theorem says and links it to the notions it is about.
A definition that coincides, definitionally or provably, with an established library object comes with a named equivalence or lemma recording the identification.
In a docstring list, a continuation line of an item is indented two spaces, under the item's text.
A class or structure field does not quantify over a universe of index types; the operation is stated on the carrier or a canonical index type, with indexed versions derived.
A few lemmas that fit an existing file (as `#find_home` reports) are added there rather than given a new file.
The general algebraic lemma is used rather than a type-specific copy of it (`zero_mul`, not `Nat.zero_mul`).
A membership characterisation `x ∈ f .. ↔ ..` is named `mem_f`, without an `_iff` suffix.
A statement about a type synonym goes through the synonym's own instances and API, not by applying the underlying type's structure across the definitional equality.
A definition written for kernel reduction or proof convenience that is slower at runtime is paired with an efficient implementation through `@[csimp]`.

A dual, additive twin, projection or characterisation lemma that a generator (`to_dual`, `to_additive`, `simps`, `mk_iff`) can produce is generated, not written by hand; the declaration is placed after the lemmas the generator needs.

A declaration deprecated in favour of one whose statement differs (in argument implicitness or form) keeps its own statement and proof under `@[deprecated]`, rather than becoming an alias of the replacement, so downstream uses keep working.
A declaration's docstring cross-references the closely related or analogous library declarations (`See also ...`).
An implicit argument that must be pinned is supplied explicitly (`@f a` or `(x := a)`), not by a type ascription on the whole term.
A notion a type may carry in several ways (a valuation, a norm) is provided as a structure as well as, or instead of, a class fixing one choice, so that several can be compared on one type.
The unqualified name of a lemma pattern (`f_const`, `f_zero`) is reserved for the unconditional statement; a version with extra hypotheses is named for them or derived from it.
A `@[simp]` lemma with side hypotheses (a conditional simp lemma) is added only with a stated reason that `simp` can discharge the hypotheses.
A goal that a lighter, more specific tactic (`omega`, `lia`, `simp`, `positivity`, `fun_prop`) or a direct lemma application closes is not closed by heavy general automation (`grind`, `aesop`).
A PR description is concise: the change and its motivation, without boilerplate sections (test plans, implementation narrative), using the repository template's syntax for dependencies.

An equality whose sides differ only in a few subterms, or a goal that a term proves up to such subterms, is closed with `convert … using n` and proofs of the differing subterms, not by rewriting one side into the other with hand-stated `show` or `have` equations.
A name carries a prime only to distinguish it from an unprimed sibling that is the primary form; a primed name with no such sibling is unprimed.

A declaration's docstring states what the value or result is in words (its defining formula or meaning), not a restatement of its type or statement; a docstring that would only repeat the statement is omitted.
Declarations about a theory are placed in that theory's established namespace, not at the root.
A constructor taking many data and proof arguments, or a hypothesis that is a long nested existential of them, takes a structure bundling them instead, so that users build it with structure syntax.
Data and conditions that serve only to state one characterisation are not made a structure; the result is stated as an iff with an existential.
A case split or lemma instantiation uses the form whose result substitutes or simplifies directly (`obtain rfl | h := eq_zero_or_pos n`), so that no hypothesis needs rewriting afterwards.
Blocks of a file are separated by a single blank line; doubled blank lines are not left.
The directions of an iff are taken with `.mp` and `.mpr`, not with the projections `.1` and `.2`.
A term derived from a person's name is spelled and capitalised as the name is (Artinian, Noetherian, von Neumann), the same way throughout the file.
The most general version of a declaration carries the plain name; a special case carries a suffix naming its specialisation (`Const`), and ad hoc suffixes such as `Dep` are not used.
A convention or exception stated in documentation gives the reason behind it, not only the rule.
Docstring terminology matches the declaration's actual generality (an element of an algebra, not an operator, when no operators are involved).
A construction built inline that is the analogue of a named library operation is extracted as its own definition under the analogous name.
Meta-code invokes a tactic's underlying function directly rather than elaborating its syntax through `evalTactic`.
A chain of equalities is written as a `calc` block, not as nested `Eq.trans` applications.
An equation used right-to-left is passed as `← h`, not first symmetrised in the context.
A PR that builds on API in the process of being deprecated or refactored uses the replacement API or waits for the refactor, rather than extending the old API.
A word in a declaration name is abbreviated the way the library abbreviates it (`Fun` for function), not ad hoc.
A test case carries a comment saying what it tests, so it is not later changed away from its purpose.
A cross-reference to another module in documentation gives its file path, not its dotted module name.
A TFAE docstring numbers its statements, so that users can refer to `out i j` without counting bullets.
A PR title follows the commit convention `type(Area): description`.
`by` ends the statement line; a proof block does not begin a line with `by`.
A lemma about the `fst`/`snd` projection of a construction names the projection postfix (`foo_apply_fst`), as `simps` generates it.
Notation, indexing and the spelling of a term for a standard notion follow the literature's usual convention; a departure is avoided or justified by a cited reference.
A local instance or definition carrying data is introduced with `let`, not `have`, which forgets the value.
Two classes carrying the same data (`InvolutiveInv`, `InvOneClass`) cannot be assumed together; a class extending both is provided for results that need both.
A new notion's name describes what the notion is; a name evoking a structure or mechanism the definition does not involve is replaced by a descriptive one.
When a refactor removes the last import across a directory boundary, the directory-dependency linter is extended to forbid that boundary, so it does not regress.
A proof term follows `:=` on the statement's line only when statement and proof together fit on one line; otherwise the proof starts on its own line.
A tactic is not given a mode that reproduces a behaviour the library tracks as technical debt, such as rewriting up to definitional unfolding as `erw` does.

A side condition on an object (a size bound, a non-degeneracy property, a dimension restriction) is a hypothesis of the lemmas that need it, not a field of a separate structure of objects satisfying it.
A `section` that would span the whole file (its variables and `open`s apply everywhere) is not opened; they are declared at file level.
A caveat about a declaration's behaviour or intended use that callers must know is stated in its docstring, and reflected in its name, not only in a comment inside its body.
A tactic that acts on hypotheses names them (`at h₁ h₂ ⊢`) rather than using `at *`.

The default binder kind in a `variable` block is the one most declarations use; a change to a `variable`'s binder kind for some declarations is scoped with `variable (x) in`, or the argument is written explicitly in those declarations, not made with a bare `variable (x)` mid-section.

An instance or a bundled morphism is given the strongest class or structure that holds (`Unique`, not `Subsingleton`, when the type is inhabited; an algebra isomorphism, not a ring isomorphism), and the weaker forms are inferred or derived from it.
A result in which one type plays two roles (scalars and coefficients, the ring and the module over it) is stated with a separate type for each role when the proof does not need them to coincide.
A cast mismatch is bridged with the cast tactics (`push_cast`, `norm_cast`, `mod_cast`), not by listing cast lemmas by hand in a `simp only` call or by a general `simpa using`.
A result bundling two facts (an `IsGreatest`, a conjunction) is also, or instead, stated as its separate component lemmas, so each is usable on its own.
Notation for a standard operation of a theory is declared `scoped` in the theory's namespace rather than `local` to one file, so other files can open it.
An `example` does not live in a library file: one exercising a tactic or extension goes in `MathlibTest`; one illustrating a definition becomes a theorem or is removed.
A `@[simp]` lemma stating an equation between composites of morphisms is tagged `@[reassoc (attr := simp)]` so the reassociated form is also a simp lemma.

A declaration's name and namespace follow the pattern of its siblings' and analogues' names (the same abbreviation of a hypothesis, the same ordering of parts, the same namespace for the same kind of construction), not a fuller or different spelling.

A declaration name or code fragment (a variable, a formula) mentioned in a comment or docstring is written in backticks and with its full name, so that it renders as code and links in the documentation.

A comment's syntax matches its role: a free-standing comment is a `/- ... -/` block, not a `/-- -/` docstring and not a run of `--` lines, and a comment describing the declaration below it is that declaration's `/-- -/` docstring.
A docstring or comment that refers to something generically ('relevant information', 'some conditions', 'the linter') names it specifically.
A lemma passed to `simp` at many call sites, always in the same direction, is tagged `@[simp]` (or made a `local simp` lemma for the file) rather than listed each time.
Declarations about one notion are grouped together, beside the existing lemmas about it, not scattered among sections or files about other notions.
A lemma named `_mono` states the one-directional monotonicity implication; the two-sided characterisation is a separate lemma named for its sides or with `_iff`.
A declaration, even a private or auxiliary one, carries a descriptive name saying what it is, not a placeholder such as `aux`.
The closing `}` of a structure-instance literal follows the last field on its line, not on a line of its own.

A declaration about a multiplicative structure comes with its additive counterpart, and one about an additive structure with its multiplicative counterpart where that exists, generated by `to_additive` when it can be and written by hand otherwise.

Induction and case analysis use the structured `induction`/`cases` syntax (`… using e with | ctor x`), which names the new variables, not the primed `induction'`/`cases'` variants or a term-mode application of the eliminator.
A lemma that holds by `rfl` is proved with the term `rfl`, not `by rfl`, so that it is tagged `@[defeq]`.
A quotient (or similarly wrapped) type exposes its own `lift`, `lift₂` and induction API, and later files go through it rather than the raw `Quotient` operations.
A pair or run of parallel one-line declarations is kept adjacent with no blank line between them, so that the parallel is visible.
Data is transported along an equality of parameters through the library's congruence equivalence (`ringEquivCongr`), not by rewriting the type with `rw` or `▸`.
A major named theorem newly formalised is recorded in the library's overview documentation (`docs/overview.md`).

A lemma's conclusion is stated about a bare variable, not a constructor application or other specific shape (a complement, an image, a pair), with any shape the proof needs moved into the hypotheses, so that the conclusion unifies with more goals.
An auxiliary top-level definition or lemma with a single use is inlined into that use rather than declared as a separate `_aux` declaration.

A file most of whose definitions are noncomputable opens one `noncomputable section` rather than marking each definition `noncomputable`; a file where only a few need it marks those definitions and does not open a section.
A lemma that is still useful as a `@[simp]` lemma is kept, not deprecated; `@[simp]` and `@[deprecated]` are not combined on one declaration.
A docstring that plays a standard role (the `toFun`/`invFun` field warning, a tactic-extension header) uses the library's established wording for that role.
A declaration is deprecated only in favour of a replacement stating the same result; when the nearest library lemma says something different, the declaration is kept.
A hypothesis that a decision procedure discharges in typical uses is given as an auto-param (`:= by lia`, `:= by simp`), so that callers need not supply it.
A binder over a set or finset (a sum, product or quantifier) is written bounded (`∑ x ∈ s, f x`, `∀ x ∈ s, p x`), not over the subtype (`∑ x : s`, `∀ x : s`) with coercions.
A docstring describes in full mathematical words (`homomorphism`, `multiplicative monoid`), not with the abbreviations used in identifiers (`hom`) or a pasted Lean expression.
A change to work that an open PR already covers is made on that PR, not opened as a duplicate PR.
An iff lemma whose name would otherwise read as the bare proposition of its left-hand side carries an `_iff` suffix, so that the name signals a characterisation.
Meta-code that handles only some of the cases its input can take fails explicitly on the others rather than silently producing output meant for a different case.

A predicate that is only meaningful under well-formedness conditions (measurability of the objects involved) includes those conditions in its definition, so that assuming the predicate suffices in later statements.
A structure whose elements are functions is given a `FunLike` instance, not a bare `CoeFun` instance, so that the generic coercion and `ext` API apply.

A type or category variable is declared with the binder that introduces fresh universe levels (`Type*`, `Category* C`), not with a fixed `Type`, a hand-declared `universe u`, or a bare `[Category C]`.
Explanation of a file's main results, and its TODO list, belong in the module docstring at the top, not in a separate comment block (`/-! -/` further down or `/- -/` after the docstring).
A lemma about a core or Batteries type (`List`, `Nat`, `Option`) that needs nothing from Mathlib is upstreamed to Lean core or Batteries rather than added to Mathlib.
A change of definition that lengthens the proofs depending on it comes with the intermediate lemmas that keep those proofs short, or a stated reason that more must now be proved.
A declaration whose name can be improved is renamed, with a deprecation for the old name; the number of deprecations is not something to minimise.
A comment flagging work to do uses the `TODO` marker, not an ad hoc marker such as `XXX`.
A `Decidable` instance that only the proofs of a definition's fields need is obtained with `classical` inside those proofs, not taken as an argument of the definition.
A structure's axiom fields are a minimal set: a field that follows from the other fields is not a field but a lemma derived from them.
Of a dependent general lemma and its non-dependent special case, `@[simp]` goes on the special case that arises in practice, not on the dependent form whose output is awkward to use.
A new file is named for the notion or result it is about and placed in that theory's directory (`Algebra.Lie.Weights.IsSimple`).
Notation is declared only when it makes statements markedly more readable than the function name; a notation that merely abbreviates a short name is not introduced.

An instance built by hand inside a proof (`let _ : Module.Free R …`, `have : Subsingleton …`), or a class-valued fact proved as a `theorem`, that holds in general is declared as a global instance, so that inference supplies it.
An instance that fixes one of several reasonable choices on a type (an order on `ℂ` or on matrices) is declared `scoped` in a named namespace (`ComplexOrder`, `Matrix.Order`), not globally.
Mathematics in a comment or docstring that unicode and backticks can express is written that way, not in LaTeX; LaTeX is reserved for formulas unicode cannot express.
A new or changed instance, linter or framework hook in a low-level file, which typeclass search or every file's elaboration will meet, is benchmarked before it is merged.
The import block is contiguous: no blank line separates the `public import`s from the `import`s.
A type, file, directory or namespace is named in the singular (`Polygon`, not `Polygons`).
A lambda whose body is a single application of its binders is written with `·` placeholder syntax or eta-reduced, not spelled out with `fun`.
The named definition is the object of interest (the iterated sequence), not an auxiliary stage of its construction (the single step) left for users to iterate.
A new general lemma or definition is applied to the existing places in the library that prove or spell its instances by hand, in the same PR or a follow-up.
A property the PR claims typeclass inference finds automatically (after a given import) is pinned by a test, so that the claim does not silently break.
A new function of a kind for which the library has a bundled type (an arithmetic function, a bundled hom) is defined as a term of that bundled type, not as a bare function.

A lemma identifying a relativised notion at its trivial parameter (`FooOn univ`) with the absolute notion is stated with the relativised side on the left and named `fooOn_univ`, as `continuousOn_univ` is.
A file below `Mathlib.Init` that cannot import it imports the header linter directly, as the other such files do, so its copyright header and module docstring are still checked.
A definition bundling an operation as a map carries the library's suffix for the kind of map it is (`ₗ` linear, `L` continuous linear, `ₐ` algebra), matching the bundle it actually returns.
A lemma that singles out one of a pair of symmetric arguments carries a `_left`/`_right` suffix naming the side, so that the lemma for the other side can be named beside it.

A `rfl` lemma whose two sides are not reducibly definitionally equal is a warning sign: the definitions are arranged so that the identification holds reducibly, since `dsimp` and unification downstream rely on it.
A statement is phrased with the notion standard for its setting (measurability outside Bochner integration), not with a stronger or more specialised notion that happens to be available.

An element of a quotient is case-analysed with the quotient's induction principle (`induction x using Quotient.inductionOn`), not destructured with `obtain ⟨x⟩`, which exposes the underlying `Quot` representation.
An improvement deferred to a later PR (a helper not yet available) is recorded as a `TODO` comment at the site it will change.
A backticked code fragment in documentation is kept on one line; line breaks fall between fragments, not inside one.
A characterisation lemma (`foo_iff`, an equation) that `grind` can use as a rewrite rule is tagged `@[grind =]`.
The `Tags` section of a module docstring lists the mathematical names users would search for, not identifiers or coined phrases.
A statement relating two propositions or predicates is an `↔` (pointwise if needed), not an equality of `Prop`s or of `Prop`-valued functions.

Meta-code that must run without a given instance disables it in a scoped environment (`withoutModifyingEnv` with `Attribute.erase`) rather than threading a flag through the elaborator to skip synthesis.
The import block is sorted alphabetically.
The module docstring's main-results list names only the substantial results; routine unfolding lemmas (`_zero`, `_succ`) are left out.
A docstring's text begins on the `/--` line, not on the line after it.

A `refine` introduces the hypotheses of its subgoals in the term (`refine ⟨fun h ↦ ?_, fun h ↦ ?_⟩`, `refine foo (fun x hx ↦ ?_)`), rather than leaving `∀`-goals for a following `intro` or using `constructor` followed by `intro`.
A lemma stating that a construction preserves a function property (continuity, measurability, differentiability) is tagged `@[fun_prop]`, so that `fun_prop` proves such goals.

A special-purpose tool or piece of meta-code that a planned general mechanism would subsume is not merged; the general solution is pursued instead, so the stopgap's maintenance burden is not taken on.
New code calls a tactic by its current name, not by a superseded alias (`cat_disch`, not `aesop_cat`).
A condition that a canonical morphism is invertible is stated as `IsIso` of that morphism, not as the existence of an isomorphism between its source and target.
A lemma registered in a simp set is stated in the direction it rewrites, so that it is tagged without `←`.
A goal that a decision procedure (`ring`, `omega`) closes is closed by it, not by its normalising variant (`ring_nf`), whose normal form is not stable.
A PR changes existing code only where its purpose requires; incidental rewrites of proofs or renames of declarations it does not need to touch are left out.
A structure's data field has the plain type, with the conditions on it as separate proof fields, not a subtype that bundles the condition into the data.
A property of a whole type (a topological or measurable space) is named with the `Space` suffix (`LocallyContractibleSpace`), as the library's other such predicates are.
Declarations needing different typeclass assumptions are organised in sections that declare exactly what each needs, not one section whose surplus assumptions are removed with `omit`.
A PR of LLM-generated code that its submitter cannot themselves understand and revise is closed rather than reviewed; review effort goes to contributors who learn from it.

A lemma whose statement builds an instance locally with `letI` is replaced by one phrased in terms of the data already present (an `_iff_edist` characterisation), so that it does not depend on one instance construction.
Several equivalent characterisations of one notion are collected in a `List.TFAE` statement, from which the pairwise iffs are derived.
A construction that recurs across many statements in an area is given its own named definition, with its API, rather than being spelled out inline each time.
A bulleted list in a docstring is separated from the surrounding paragraphs by a blank line.
A declaration is not stated in a generality (semilinear maps, extra parameters) that no use needs when that generality complicates the statement; it is generalised when a use arrives.
A variable bound in a declaration's signature is given an explicit type, not left for elaboration to infer from its uses.
The dual of an order-theoretic lemma is proved by instantiating the original at the order dual (`αᵒᵈ`), not by repeating its proof.
A declaration stated with `theorem` rather than `lemma` is one important enough to carry a docstring; `theorem` is not used for an undocumented auxiliary result.
A structure field with an auto-param default that the default tactic discharges is omitted, not supplied by hand.
Among equivalent definitions, the one whose basic characterisation lemmas (membership, application) hold by `rfl` is chosen.
A result taken from a tagged reference database (the Stacks project) carries the corresponding tag attribute (`@[stacks]`), naming the part of the entry it proves.
A docstring describes the declaration it is attached to; overview text about a design or framework goes on its central declaration or in the module docstring.
A goal `a ≠ b` or `¬ p` is proved by introducing the hypothesis directly (`rintro rfl`, `intro h`), not by `by_contra`.
An equation produced by destructuring is substituted with the `rfl` pattern (`obtain ⟨n, rfl⟩`), not named and rewritten with afterwards.
Variables of the same kind declared in one `variable` command are grouped in a single binder (`{α β γ : Type*}`), not split into several binders of that type.
A hypothesis named in a lemma name is introduced by the connective `of` (`foo_of_bar`), as the library's naming convention spells it, not an ad hoc word such as `if`.
Deprecated declarations that no longer have a home in the file they came from are moved to a file under `Mathlib/Deprecated/`, not kept in the live file or deleted.
A definition meant to be reducible is declared with `abbrev`, not with `@[reducible] def`.
Parallel arguments of a statement carry the same strength of assumption (both `Finite` or both `Fintype`), as callers will have them, not a mixture.
Of several equivalent formulations of a notion, the one easiest to use in practice is made the definition and the others are characterisation lemmas.
A tactic proof of more than a line is not embedded as `by ...` inside an anonymous-constructor term; the term is given with `refine` and `?_` and the proof follows on its own lines.
A statement does not carry a vacuous hypothesis (`x ∈ univ`); the binder is left unbounded.
A relativised notion (`FooOn s`, `FooAt x`) comes with the absolute predicate (`Foo`, meaning `FooOn univ`), as the library provides for `Continuous`.
A lemma added by a PR is used in it, registered with an attribute, or part of its intended API; a lemma that is none of these is removed.
A lemma whose statement is of independent use is public API, not `private`; `private` is reserved for lemmas that serve one proof or expose an implementation.
A module docstring says only what helps a reader of this file; boilerplate copied from sibling files, such as a list of variable-name conventions, is left out.
A new notion that refines or parallels an existing one comes with the analogues of the existing notion's API lemmas.
Rewriting that only normalises the goal before the main argument is done before a `calc` block, not as the block's first step.
In a `module` file, an instance, and any declaration downstream files need, is marked `public`; an unmarked declaration is invisible to importers.
A hypothesis or conclusion is spelled in the form the library's existing lemmas use most; when another spelling is kept, lemmas relating the two spellings are provided.
A generator attribute (`to_additive`, `to_fun`, `to_dual`) is given an explicit target name only when that name differs from the one the generator would produce.
A notation is declared at a precedence (`:max`) that lets it stand as a function argument without parentheses.
Local instances that a dedicated tactic installs (`algebraize`, `classical`) are introduced by that tactic, not by hand with `letI`/`haveI` one at a time.
A class or structure that asserts a property of an object is named with the `Is` prefix (`IsPolynormableSpace`).
A class or structure whose fields are all propositions is declared `: Prop` explicitly.
A `variable` command, and a section around it, serves an argument shared by many declarations; an argument used by one declaration or only a few is bound in their signatures.
A step that every branch of a case split performs is done once before the split, not repeated in each branch.
A hypothesis is named after the variable it constrains (`hc : c ≠ 0`), not with a name carried over from a sibling about a different variable.
A definition that builds a typeclass instance but is deliberately not an `instance` is an `abbrev` carrying the `-- see Note [reducible non-instances]` comment.
The fields after `where` are indented two spaces under the declaration keyword, not four.
A PR containing AI-generated code is cleaned up by its submitter before review: narrative comments, convoluted arguments and non-terminal `simp`s are removed as a human author would remove them.

A lemma stating a bundled function property (`Function.Injective f`, `Monotone f`) is named with the property's full word (`f_injective`, `f_monotone`), and its unbundled pointwise form (`f a = f b ↔ a = b`, `a ≤ b → f a ≤ f b`) with the short form (`f_inj`, `f_mono`), as the naming guide prescribes.
An improvement to a tactic's behaviour is made the tactic's default rather than offered as a `!` variant, unless the old behaviour is still needed.
A lemma takes a witness and its properties as separate arguments (`e`, `he : e ∈ E`, `hx : x ∈ e`) rather than one existential hypothesis, so that callers apply it without packaging.

An implementation note warning that a definition clashes with another instance or definition says precisely how the two differ (a mathematically distinct operation built from different data, not a definitional diamond), not merely that they conflict.
A definition that fixes a special case of a broader notion (random variables on one probability space) states that restriction in its docstring and says what to use in the general case.
A numeral or coercion whose type is not evident from its context (`↑0`) carries a type ascription saying what it is.
An equality used to rewrite the goal is stated as a `suffices` or `have` and rewritten with, not proved inside a `conv ... equals` block.
A comment or docstring recording that a declaration was adapted from, or is similar to, another in-library declaration is not kept.
A term of an option-like type (`WithBot ℕ`, `ℕ∞`) known to be finite is brought down to the base type with `lift`, not case-split with the impossible case handled by hand.
The explicit arguments of a declaration are ordered with the term that dot notation applies to first and the remaining data after it.
An existence result whose witness is canonical is given as a definition of the witness and lemmas about it, with the existential statement derived as a corollary.
A `section`, file or directory is named after the notion its declarations are about, spelled as that notion's declaration spells it.

A function-property goal (continuity, analyticity) that `fun_prop` almost closes is closed by `fun_prop` with the missing facts put in the context and a discharger supplied, not by hand-applying the structural lemmas (`.add`, `.mul`, `.div`).
A structure whose data includes an existing bundled structure `extends` it rather than carrying it as a named field, so that the parent's projections and coercions apply.
An `Iff` theorem is proved with `constructor` or the anonymous constructor, not with `where mp := ... mpr := ...` field syntax, which reads as a definition.
Meta-code that tests whether two expressions agree uses a definitional-equality check at reducible transparency (`withReducible isDefEq`), not syntactic equality (`==`).

Of two overlapping lemmas about one definition, a map-level `_apply` and its pointwise `_apply_apply`, `@[simp]` goes on the one whose output is the more useful form, not on the fully applied one by default.
A hypothesis whose type is a class (`IsEmpty`, `Nonempty`, `Fact`) is taken as an instance-implicit argument `[C x]`, not as a named explicit hypothesis.
A type-specific lemma is deprecated for its general algebraic counterpart only when the typeclass search the general lemma triggers at each use is an acceptable cost.
A `private` or auxiliary lemma carries a docstring saying what it is for, so that the reason it exists need not be hunted for.
A finiteness assumption or instance used only as a proposition is `Finite`, not `Fintype`; a noncomputable `Fintype` instance is not declared where `Finite` serves.
A docstring that is a noun phrase rather than a complete sentence does not end with a full stop.
A trace, log or error message emitted by meta-code is a neutral statement of what happened (`found X for Y`), not a colloquial remark.
A function given as a chain of compositions (`f ∘ g ∘ h`) in a statement is written as an explicit lambda (`fun x ↦ f (g (h x))`).
A PR that arises from a public discussion (a Zulip thread) links that discussion in its description.

A class or structure involving a carrier type that has its own instances (a category, a ring) takes that type and its instances as parameters, not as fields, so that identifications with existing types hold syntactically rather than by forced definitional unfolding.

A goal that is a lemma's conclusion up to simp-normalisation is closed by `simpa using` the lemma applied to explicit arguments, not by rewriting the goal backwards with `←` simp lemmas into the lemma's form.
The name or design of a new concept is settled by community consensus (a Zulip discussion) before the PR is merged, not chosen by the author alone.
An identification of two objects of a category is provided as an isomorphism (a `def`), not stated as an equality of objects.
A new definition, structure or instance that introduces a notion carries a docstring saying what it is.
A degenerate parameter (a zero-dimensional space, a trivial index) is written as the canonical trivial type (`Unit`), not as a degenerate instance of a general family (`EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 0)`).
The copyright line of a file header names the holder in the canonical form the library's other headers use.
A bibliography entry reproduces the BibTeX of the standard reference database (Math Reviews) rather than a hand-corrected variant.

When a generator (`to_additive`, `to_dual`) produces a declaration from another, both carry docstrings: the original its own, and the generated one through the attribute; neither is left undocumented.

A declaration's arguments are ordered from the ambient setting inward: typeclass assumptions on the ambient structures first, then the data (functors, objects), then the hypotheses about specific objects.
A trace message that serves only to debug the meta-code itself is emitted under the detailed trace class, not the class users enable for ordinary output.
A rewrite in a proof is done with `rw` (or a lemma application), not with the `▸` substitution, which hides what is rewritten.
In a `calc` block whose steps align their `:=` in a column, every step is aligned to that column.

A lemma about objects with a property is stated for the general type with the property as a typeclass hypothesis (`Measure` with `IsFiniteMeasure`), not for the bundled subtype of such objects, whose API is not duplicated.
A coercion of a bundled map to a function is written with the `⇑` arrow, not with a type ascription `(f : X → Y)`.
When a directory is created for the notion a file is about, that file moves into the directory as `Basic.lean` rather than staying beside it.
A statement is written with `<` and `≤`, not `>` and `≥`.
A hypothesis `a < b` is named in the orientation (`lt` or `gt`) that reads its variables in the order they appear in the conclusion.

The cases of a custom induction or recursion principle are stated at their simplest: a case that another case already extends (stability under isomorphism from an exactness case) is stated only for the canonical representative.
A lemma does not take an equation `x = f y` as a hypothesis; it is stated with `f y` in place of `x`, and a caller rewrites its goal before applying it.
A lemma about a function property is named by the naming guide's convention for the expanded (`fun x ↦ f x + g x`) and unexpanded (`f + g`) forms of its function.
The docstring of a definition formalising a named mathematical notion points to background reading on it (a reference or an encyclopedia link).
Notation namespaces are opened with `open scoped`, on their own command, and are not merged into an `open` of declaration namespaces.
A hypothesis is stated in the form easiest for a caller to supply (`n ≠ 0` rather than `0 < n`); the stronger form is reserved for conclusions.

Specific values of a sequence or function (small Bernoulli numbers) are not added as lemmas value by value; a general mechanism for computing them (an efficient algorithm, a `norm_num` extension or simproc) is provided so that any value can be obtained when needed.
A run of trailing `_` placeholders in an application is written as `..`, not as several underscores.

A `rfl` proof of an identification that downstream unification and `dsimp` rely on is written `with_reducible_and_instances rfl`, so that the defeq is checked, and seen to hold, at reducible transparency.
A docstring does not describe a map as 'canonical'; it names the map (the inclusion, the quotient map) or leaves the adjective out, and does so consistently across a file.
An import that every file carries for its side effect (a linter) is listed once in the import-shaking tool's globally-ignored set, not exempted file by file.
A predicate or function on a quotient type is defined by lifting the corresponding one on representatives through `Quotient.lift` with its invariance proof, not by quantifying over representatives.
A deprecated alias stays until its deprecation period ends; a further rename adds a new alias and retargets the existing one rather than removing or reusing its name.
In a `module` file, `@[expose]` is placed on the individual definitions whose bodies downstream files must unfold, not on the whole public section.
An equation lemma is named for its left-hand side, or as `lhs_eq_rhs` naming both sides; a bare `_eq` suffix naming no right-hand side is not used.
The module docstring of a file proving a substantial theorem outlines the strategy of the proof and names the main ingredients it draws on.
A deprecation records its date in the attribute's `since` field, not in a trailing comment.
A test of a tactic's core mechanism imports only the tactic's core and declares locally the attributes it needs, so that it does not depend on the library's registered attribute set.
A lemma stating that a construction takes equal values on equivalent or isomorphic inputs (`f α = f β` from `α ≃ β`) is named `f_congr`, not `f_eq`.
A `have` inside a proof is placed immediately before the first step that uses it, not earlier in the proof.
A result stated for a degenerate special case (the trivial object) is stated for the broadest natural class to which it extends (all finite objects) when the general proof is within reach.
